extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of sociology, cultural/media studies, and humour research
extracted.subtask_description: Theoretical guidance for analyzing humour and ridicule in mass media, politics, and everyday culture, including ethical, political and sociological dimensions of comedic practice and reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continual tone of irreverence in mass media
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass (popular) media is characterized by a continual tone of irreverence: within the daily carnival of television are comics who parody and satirize the recognizable figures of the day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parody of celebrities by celebrity comics both mocks and confirms celebrity status — the fact of being parodied validates a target as sufficiently important. Use observations of routine parody to evaluate the cultural role and normalisation of irreverence in media contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspend humour after major collective tragedies
rubrics_metrics.description: The ordinary carnival might be interrupted by exceptional, brief periods of cessation following dramatic moments of tragedy (e.g., death of Princess Diana, 9/11): it was deemed inappropriate to show humorous programmes on television for a short period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an irregular, unforeseen collective seriousness not built into calendars. When assessing appropriateness, consider whether the context is such an exceptional moment that humour would be judged socially unacceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility of humour with capitalist market demands
rubrics_metrics.description: A constant carnival of fun fits well with contemporary capitalism which must constantly revolutionize itself — production, marketing and products must be updated; consumers must be left in a continual state of desire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate humour for how it reflects or reinforces commercial imperatives: mocking what is outdated, encouraging desire for the new, and aligning with advertising practices that ridicule lack of advertised products. Consider whether humour functions to reproduce consumerist elasticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural preference for 'naughtiness' over stuffiness
rubrics_metrics.description: In this cultural climate few would wish to appear stuffy, old-fashioned or puritan; the position of the naughty child is more comfortable and desirable than the humourless, disciplinarian parent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing performers/personae, assess the value placed on youthful naughtiness (e.g., self-deprecatory or mischievous styles) and the avoidance of being perceived as prudish or haughty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebellious humour can perform conservative functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparently rebellious humour can fulfil conservative functions: when the market dictates constant revolution, conformists can appear to have radical jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of claims that transgressive jokes are politically radical; examine whether 'rebellious' humour actually sustains existing power structures or market logics rather than challenging them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Left-wing comedy disadvantaged by enforcement of respectful codes
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics on the left can be in a difficult position because the left often insists on codes of speech (against ableist, homophobic, xenophobic terms), which can make conservative comedians appear daring by flouting such codes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating political humour, consider how normative speech codes shape reception: anti-pattern is to accept 'it's only a joke' as sufficient defence. Assess whether transgression is genuinely emancipatory or merely performance of rebelliousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jeering requires lack of compassion (ethical cost of mockery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jeering requires a lack of compassion — an 'anaesthesia of the heart' — and laughter at those seeking compassion is easier than vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include ethical assessment of humour that targets vulnerable groups or invokes jeering; measure humour's moral costs by whether it diminishes compassion or cruelly marginalizes targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Morality of humour determined by purposes, not form
rubrics_metrics.description: The outward form of humour can serve different tendentious purposes; 'the morality comes not from the humour itself but from the purposes to which it is put.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging humour, focus on intent, function and consequences rather than intrinsic properties of comic forms. Use contextual analysis to determine whether humour advances harmful or beneficial ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialectic between humour and seriousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour and seriousness are necessarily linked in a dialectic (oscillation between freedom and necessity, pleasure and duty); neither can abolish the other without abolishing itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses should account for interplay: humour can discipline seriousness and seriousness can be subverted by mockery. Avoid binary judgments that privilege one over the other without considering mutual dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and ending influence comedic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Within particular contexts there can be a last moment of humour or seriousness: some stand-up comedians reserve their best jokes until last to leave amid appreciative laughter; others end with a seriously delivered, sentimental song.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate structure and dramaturgy of comedic acts (pacing, placement of punchlines, choice of final tone). Consider how endings shape audience interpretation and the perceived purpose of the act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour as disciplinary force against bodily inelasticity
rubrics_metrics.description: Following Bergson, humour operates as a weapon of the spirit against the inelasticity of the body; however, it cannot break free from the body since it requires the bodily reaction of laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess humour's role in policing or correcting rigid social or bodily norms, and note the embodied nature of humour (laughter as response). Use this to analyze functions of mockery that aim to discipline behaviour.
